response.explanation: The removed canViewGlobal short-circuit is redundant. In GroupPermissions.canView(GroupModel), the first check is canView() || canManage(), which is the global check. In GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel), the same admin-role check comes first. After that, hasPermission falls back to the group-type resource when no per-group resource exists. The call to session.groups().searchGroupsByAttributes exists in GroupLookupProvider and has the same signature as the helper it replaces. The change from GroupModel child = null to GroupModel child is harmless.
response.title: No defect found in group listing/subgroup permission refactor

response.consequence: A read-only (view) admin can create top-level groups and move existing groups to top level via POST on the groups endpoint. This is privilege escalation from view to manage.
response.explanation: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() calls hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE), so an admin granted only the 'view' scope on the all-groups resource type returns true. canManage(GroupModel) correctly checks only MANAGE. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage(), which relies on the no-arg canManage(). It then creates groups, or moves an existing group to top level by id. The interface Javadoc was edited to describe this VIEW-or-MANAGE behavior, so the docs also encode the flaw.
response.title: No-arg canManage() accepts view-only scope, allowing group creation

response.explanation: The removed java.util.Arrays import in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest is not used anywhere in that file. The new group test's helper methods are defined in the same file.
response.title: No defect found

response.consequence: No defect that this change introduces was found in impersonation evaluation. The target-user binding was already there, is unchanged by this diff, and matches the legacy behavior.
response.explanation: canImpersonate does build its EvaluationContext from new UserModelIdentity(root.realm, user), the target user. The diff does not touch that method, and the legacy UserPermissions.isImpersonatable (UserPermissions.java:402) builds its context the same way. When requester is null, hasPermission passes a null context, and evaluation then falls back to the admin identity in MgmtPermissions.evaluatePermission (line 331). I could not show a defect the change introduces. The other edits in the diff are the dropped ADMIN role and the added canManageByGroup fallbacks. I found nothing wrong in them. I did not read the tests, and I did not confirm that the ADMIN role is covered through composite roles.
response.title: Impersonation context binding is not introduced by this change

response.consequence: Users who have view-members permission on a specific group do not see that group in filtered listings. Users with only an all-groups permission get every resource UUID back, and none of those match a real group ID. Group listings are filtered incorrectly.
response.explanation: AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates group resources with the group's ID as the resource name (resolveGroup returns group.getId(); resourceStore.create(server, name, ...)). The resource's own getId() is a separate generated UUID. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission, which calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), so the lookup returns null. It then falls back to the generic "all-groups" type resource. The per-group permission is therefore never evaluated. The code also adds groupResource.getId() (the resource UUID) to the result set instead of the group ID, so the returned values are not group IDs.
response.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses resource ID where the group ID (resource name) is required

response.consequence: No confirmed NullPointerException path in normal use. The unguarded dereference is only a theoretical risk if the type resource were removed out of band.
response.explanation: getResourceTypeResource returns null only when the schema is unsupported, the type is unknown, or the type resource is missing. The first case needs the realm's admin permissions to be disabled or the server to belong to a different realm. hasPermission is reached only through V2 with the realm's own permissions resource server, and it returns early when isAdminSameRealm is false or realmResourceServer is null. AdminPermissionsSchema.init creates the groups, users and clients type resources together with the admin permissions client. GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE is a known type. I found no path that deletes the type resource while the V2 evaluator is active.
response.title: No reachable null from getResourceTypeResource in hasPermission

response.explanation: The removed `!auth.users().canView()` guard in searchForUser is now inside `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`, which returns an empty set when `root.users().canView()` is true. The behavior is the same, and results are still filtered with `usersEvaluator::canView`. `canViewDefault` and `canManageDefault` were inlined with the same role checks. `canViewByGroup` now calls `canViewMembers`, and `AdminPermissions.registerListener` now checks the feature flag once when the listener is registered.

hypotheses.evidence_needed: Confirm that the VIEW scope is accepted in the no-arg canManage() path. Show a caller that grants a mutation to a view-only admin. A test that grants only 'view' on the Groups type and then calls a manage endpoint would settle it.
hypotheses.failure_mode: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() calls hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE). An admin who holds only the 'view' scope on the all-groups resource type therefore passes canManage(). This is privilege escalation from view to manage for group operations that use the no-arg canManage(). The interface Javadoc says canManage() should require manage permission.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: Compare canManage() with canManage(GroupModel), which correctly passes only MANAGE. Then find the callers of the no-arg canManage() and requireManage(), such as group creation and rename, and check whether a view-only permission reaches them.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: An authorization check that is too permissive lets a read-only admin write.

hypotheses.evidence_needed: A resource's id and name differ, and findByName(resource.getId()) returns null. Or a test with a per-group view-members permission shows the wrong set of group IDs.
hypotheses.failure_mode: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() iterates resources from findByType and passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission(). hasPermission() looks the group up with resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). Resource names are group IDs, but the resource ID is a different value. The lookup returns null, so every group falls back to the all-groups type resource. The result is either all groups or none, ignoring per-group view-members permissions.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: Check what name the V2 schema gives group resources (getOrCreateResource uses the group id as the name). Check whether Resource.getId() differs from getName(). Then trace how the returned set filters group listings.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: Wrong filtering of group listings can leak group existence or hide permitted groups.

hypotheses.evidence_needed: A path where getResourceTypeResource returns null while the V2 evaluator is active, for example after the resource is deleted or when the realm's permission client is not yet initialized. An unguarded dereference confirms it.
hypotheses.failure_mode: In hasPermission() the fallback getResourceTypeResource(...) can return null when the Groups type resource is missing or the schema is unsupported. policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and resource.getScopes() then throw a NullPointerException instead of denying.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: Check whether the Groups type resource always exists once admin permissions are enabled. Check the order of realm creation and permission-client setup, and what getResourceTypeResource returns on its null paths.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: A NullPointerException in an authorization check turns a deny into a 500 error. It is reachable from many group endpoints.

hypotheses.evidence_needed: Show that the policy is evaluated with the target user's identity rather than the admin's. A test where only the admin matches the user policy, or only the target does, shows the wrong decision.
hypotheses.failure_mode: UserPermissionsV2.canImpersonate builds the EvaluationContext from new UserModelIdentity(root.realm, user), which is the target user, not the calling admin (root.identity). Policies are therefore evaluated against the impersonated user's identity, so impersonation could be granted or denied for the wrong subject. When requester is null the context is null and the default identity is used.
hypotheses.investigation_rationale: Compare with the legacy isImpersonatable, which also uses the user identity. Check what the V2 impersonate permission is meant to bind to. Read the rest of hasPermission and how it uses the context. Look at the tests for impersonate permissions.
hypotheses.priority_rationale: Impersonation is among the most sensitive admin capabilities, and an identity mix-up could grant or deny it incorrectly.
